1: Welcome to Data Two Oh Nine, Advanced Exploratory Data Analysis. This is Module One, where we build the foundations. In these first two lectures we will learn how to take raw data and turn it into numbers you can actually trust. The course is taught at Vidyashilp University by Doctor Shital Bhatt.
2: Here is the plan for the next two lectures: six ideas. Lecture one covers where exploration sits in a data science project, the difference between exploratory and confirmatory analysis, and sampling bias. Lecture two covers summary statistics, the shape of a distribution, meaning skewness, kurtosis and outliers, and finally robust statistics like the median and the I Q R. Keep this list in mind, because every later module builds on these six ideas.
3: Lecture one. The title says it all: why we explore before we conclude. Today we look at the data science lifecycle, the two very different jobs of exploration and confirmation, and how a biased sample can ruin an analysis before it even begins.
4: The main idea of this lecture is simple. Exploratory analysis is detective work, and confirmatory analysis is the trial. A detective looks at clues with an open mind and forms theories. A trial tests one specific accusation under strict rules. John Tukey introduced exploratory data analysis in nineteen seventy seven. His point was that we should look at data using pictures and resistant summaries, so that the data can surprise us. A good picture forces you to notice something you were not looking for.
5: Many beginners think exploration is stage two: you load the data, explore a little, and then move on to modelling. This slide says that is wrong. Exploration runs through the whole lifecycle. At every step, from collecting data to deploying a model, you ask a question and answer it by looking at the data. And every decision that comes out of it should be one you can defend in your report.
6: So what does exploration actually give you? Five concrete jobs. First, sanity: does the file contain what the documentation claims, in terms of rows, column types, units and dates? Second, quality: missing values, duplicates, impossible values, and missing data hidden as zero, minus one or nine ninety nine. Third, structure: shapes of variables, relationships between pairs, clusters, trends and seasonality. Fourth, hypotheses: candidate explanations that are worth testing later, on data you have not looked at yet. And fifth, modelling decisions: which transformations, which features, which model family, and what the baseline should be.
7: Here is a worked example from the Pima diabetes dataset, with seven hundred sixty eight patients. A quick describe shows that glucose, blood pressure, skin thickness, insulin and B M I all have a minimum of zero. That is medically impossible for a living patient. These values were never actually zero. The missing values had been encoded as zero. Only pregnancies can genuinely be zero, so we leave that one alone. If you trained a model on this file without checking, roughly half the insulin column would be the number zero, and the model would learn that having no test predicts health. No amount of tuning fixes that. Five minutes of exploration does.
8: Now let us compare the two jobs side by side. Exploratory analysis asks: what is going on in this data? The hypothesis is generated by the analysis itself, you can look as many times as you like, and your tools are plots, summaries and cross tabs. The output is candidate hypotheses and cleaned data. Confirmatory analysis asks: is this specific claim supported? The hypothesis is fixed before you see the data, you get one pre specified look, and the output is a p value. Notice the valid claims. Exploratory says: conversion appears higher on weekends, which is worth testing. Confirmatory says: conversion is higher, with a p value of point zero zero four. The fatal mistake in exploration is refusing to look and modelling blind. The fatal mistake in confirmation is testing a hypothesis that the same data suggested.
9: How do professionals keep these two jobs apart? Four habits. One, split the data first. Hold out a confirmation set before you plot anything, explore on the other part, and touch the held out rows only once, at the end. Two, write the hypothesis down before testing: the outcome, the comparison, the direction and the test. A dated note or a commit is enough, as long as it comes before the result. Three, label every claim in your report as exploratory or confirmatory, so readers know which is which. Four, if you must run many tests on one dataset, use false discovery rate control. That is a repair, not a replacement for planning. In this course, your final project must state for each headline claim whether it was exploratory or confirmatory.
10: Next, sampling. People say the data, but there are actually four different things. The target population is everyone the claim is about, for example all potential customers of a website. The sampling frame is the list you could actually draw from, for example everyone who reached the site and got a session cookie. The sample is the rows you ended up with, here twelve thousand three hundred thirty sessions. And the estimate is the number you compute, here a conversion rate of fifteen point five percent. The gap between population and frame is called coverage error. The Online Shoppers data has no row for a person who never visited, so it can tell you how visitors behave, but nothing about why others stayed away. Before any analysis, write one sentence: this sample can support claims about blank, and cannot support claims about blank.
11: There are six common ways a sample stops representing its population. Selection bias: the way rows got into the file is related to the outcome, like surveying only app users about app satisfaction. Self selection: people choose whether to appear, like product reviews, where delighted and furious customers write but the indifferent majority does not. Survivorship bias: failures are missing from the data entirely, like studying only companies that still exist today. Non response bias: selected people do not answer, and that relates to the answer, like busy doctors skipping a workload survey. Undercoverage: a group is systematically absent, like telephone polls missing homes without phones. And measurement bias: the instrument itself is skewed, like a tracker that ignores sessions shorter than three seconds, silently deleting every bounce.
12: Two cases worth remembering. In nineteen thirty six, the Literary Digest magazine mailed about ten million ballots, got over two million replies, and still predicted the wrong winner of the American presidential election. Their address lists came from telephone directories, club rosters and car registrations, which in the Depression leaned wealthy, and only the motivated replied. That is undercoverage plus non response. Two million biased answers lost to a few thousand well drawn ones. The second case is from the Second World War. Analysts mapped bullet holes on returning planes and proposed armouring the most damaged areas. Abraham Wald pointed out the flaw: they only saw planes that came back. Holes were rare on the engines because planes hit there never returned. That is survivorship bias. So always ask of every dataset: what would a row look like that could never have been recorded?
13: Now a second big idea: two ways of being wrong, bias and variance. A useful way to remember it: bias is where you aim, and variance is how steady your hand is.
14: Picture a dartboard. Low bias means your darts are centred on the bullseye on average. High bias means they cluster away from it. Low variance means the darts are tightly grouped, and high variance means they are scattered. The best case is low bias and low variance. The worst place to be is the top right, high bias and low variance: wrong, and confident about it, because the darts are tightly grouped in the wrong place.
15: Let us define them. Bias is systematic error. You are consistently off in the same direction, so if you repeat the whole exercise, you make the same mistake again. Examples: a weighing scale that reads two hundred grams heavy, a survey that only willing people answer, or a straight line fitted to a curved pattern. Bias does not shrink with more data. Variance is random error. You are off in an unpredictable direction, so repeating the exercise gives a different answer each time. Examples: two samples of fifty giving two different means, a decision tree whose shape changes with the data, or noise mistaken for a pattern. Variance does shrink as data grows, roughly like one over the square root of n. Total error is the part that repeats plus the part that reshuffles.
16: This chart shows the asymmetry. As the sample grows from one hundred to ten thousand, the random error curve falls, but slowly. Four times the data only halves it. The systematic error, the flat amber line, never moves. So past a certain point, collecting more data only shrinks the error you were not worried about. This is why more data is not always the answer.
17: The same two ideas appear in two senses. First, in your data. Bias means the sample is systematically unlike the population, for example only satisfied customers reply to the feedback link. Variance means the sample is fair but small, so it wobbles. Fifty random customers give three point nine stars, another fifty give four point two. The key message: a big biased sample is more dangerous than a small random one, because it arrives with a narrow margin of error, so the wrong answer looks precise. Size buys confidence, not correctness.
18: Second, in your model. A model that is too simple has high bias and low variance. A straight line cannot follow a curve, and it is wrong in the same way on every dataset. A model that is about right follows the real shape and ignores the jitter, and different data gives a similar model. A model that is too flexible has low bias and high variance. It passes through every point including the noise, and different data gives a wildly different model. These are the same ten data points in all three pictures. The only thing that changed is how much freedom the model was given.
19: Where does a prediction's error come from? Expected error equals bias squared, plus variance, plus irreducible noise. Bias squared is how far the average model sits from the truth. You fix it by adding capacity, such as more features or a richer model. Variance is how much the model moves when the data changes. You fix it by removing freedom, with regularisation, pruning or more training data. And noise is the randomness the world simply contains. No model can fix it. It sets the floor on how good you can get. The first two you can trade against each other. The third is not negotiable.
20: This is why there is a sweet spot. On the left, with simple models, bias dominates and we underfit. On the right, with flexible models, variance dominates and we overfit. The total error on unseen data, the dark curve, is U shaped. The bottom of that U is where we want to be, and cross validation is how we find it.
21: How do you tell which problem you have? With high bias, training error is high, and test error is high and close to the training error. Adding more data barely helps. You need a richer model, better features, or less regularisation. With high variance, training error is very low but test error is much higher. More data helps a lot. You need a simpler model, more regularisation, or more data. The quickest test: does the gap between training and test error worry you more than the level of both?
22: One important caution. The bias variance trade off is about estimation, not collection. Regularisation, cross validation and more training rows all work on the error inside your model. None of them repairs a sample that never contained the people you care about. The result can be perfectly repeatable and perfectly wrong. Sampling bias is fixed at the design stage, or not at all.
23: Remember this much. Bias repeats, variance reshuffles. Bias is being wrong the same way every time. Variance is being wrong differently every time. More data shrinks variance and leaves bias exactly where it was. In models, complexity trades one for the other and total error is U shaped. In samples, only better design fixes bias. No amount of tuning will.
24: To recap lecture one, carry forward three things. Exploration is a habit that recurs at every stage, not a box to tick before modelling. Exploration generates hypotheses, confirmation tests them, never on the same rows. And sample size fixes noise, but only sample design fixes bias.
